title: Introducing Tools in an Organisation
concept:
Introducing a test tool is a project in itself. Done well, it pays back. Done badly, it generates expensive shelf-ware.

**Selection phase**:
- Identify the problem the tool will solve (don't start with 'we need automation').
- Survey candidate tools — short-list 3–5 based on technical fit, cost, vendor stability, community.
- Define evaluation criteria: features, performance, integration, learning curve, total cost of ownership (licence + training + maintenance), support quality.
- Pilot the top 2–3 on a representative real problem. Measure objectively.
- Buy-in from sponsors and the test team.

**Adoption phase**:
- **Pilot project** — apply the tool on a small, real, low-risk project. Capture lessons.
- **Training** — formal training plus hands-on mentoring.
- **Coaching** — embed an expert (internal or vendor) in early projects to model good usage.
- **Standards and guidelines** — naming, structure, abstractions, review checklist.
- **Roll-out plan** — gradual extension to more teams/projects, with retrospectives at each step.
- **Integration** — connect to ALM, defect tracker, CI/CD; otherwise the tool's outputs are stranded.

**Sustaining**:
- Ongoing maintenance budget, not just initial purchase.
- Periodic review: is the tool still the best fit? Is the team using it as intended?
- Reassess at major version upgrades or stack changes.

A common failure mode: pick a tool because a senior person likes it, skip the pilot, train no-one, then declare 'automation doesn't work' when adoption falters. CTFL emphasises the disciplined adoption process.
keyPoints: Tool introduction is a project: select (with pilots and objective criteria), adopt (training, coaching, standards), sustain (ongoing maintenance and reassessment).
Pilot on a representative real problem before committing; train people; integrate with ALM/CI/CD.
Common failure mode: pick by preference, skip pilot, skip training — leads to shelf-ware.

quiz.question: An organisation has chosen a new test automation tool. Which adoption activity is MOST important to perform BEFORE rolling it out to all teams?
options: Buy as many licences as possible to lock in the price.
Pilot the tool on a small, representative real project and capture lessons learned.
Re-brand the tool with the company logo.
Disable the existing test framework so teams have no alternative.
quiz.explanation: Piloting on a real but small project reveals fit, gaps, and effort before company-wide commitment. Bulk-buying licences before piloting risks shelf-ware; cosmetics and forcing adoption don't address fit or skill gaps.
